metadata.title: Socioeconomic achievement gap in Taiwan: The impact of COVID-19 on math performance

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PISA microdata for Taiwan across multiple cycles (2006, 2009, 2012, 2015, 2018, 2022) and constructs a repeated cross-sectional analytic dataset by SES group (bottom vs top quarter of ESCS) and time (pre- vs post-pandemic). The manuscript does not report whether PISA sampling weights or replicate weights were applied in the DID regressions, nor does it name any weight variables (e.g., TOTWGT or W_FSTUWT). Because the analysis is a regression-based DID with fixed effects and standard errors, analysts using the OECD PISA Data Explorer should apply the appropriate complex-survey weights and replicate weights if available in the released dataset to obtain population-representative estimates and correct uncertainty under the multistage sampling design. If weights are omitted, results should be interpreted as within-sample associations rather than fully design-representative effects, and standard errors may be understated given the clustered school/country structure.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper states that each observation represents a plausible value of a student’s test score, but it does not describe how plausible values were combined (e.g., Rubin’s rules vs averaging) or how missing data in covariates were handled. This is a reporting gap because PISA datasets typically require explicit PV combination and a documented missing-data strategy to ensure valid standard errors and unbiased estimates. Without this information, the exact inferential procedure for the DID coefficients cannot be fully audited.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used OECD PISA student performance data for Taiwan for cycles 2006, 2009, 2012, 2015, 2018, and 2022. The analytic sample is restricted to students in the bottom quarter vs top quarter of the ESCS (socioeconomic status) distribution, defining Lower=1 (bottom 25%) and Higher=0 (top 25%). The DID comparison pools pre-pandemic observations (2006–2018) versus the post-pandemic period (2022), and includes students with available values for the specified controls (gender, immigrant background, grade, setting, public/private, general/vocational) as used in the regression models. No additional exclusions (e.g., missing covariates) are explicitly described beyond the final regression sample sizes reported in Tables 3–4.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2006–2022 Taiwan (secondary students), Math achievement (Plausible Values)
main_findings.target_variable: Math achievement gap (Lower × Post DID interaction)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Difference-in-differences (DID) regression, Model 2: Lower×Post β = -26.110 (s.e. 7.928), p < 0.01; Model 0: β = -17.136 (s.e. 8.348), p < 0.05; Model 1: β = -19.028 (s.e. 8.373), p < 0.05. Descriptive DID estimate for math: -17.60 (s.e. 0.20), p < 0.01. R² (Model 2): 0.326.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2006–2022 Taiwan the study leveraged socioeconomic status (ESCS) group membership (Lower vs Higher) and the post-pandemic indicator (Post) to estimate the DID effect on math achievement, finding that the Lower×Post interaction was negative and statistically significant (about a 26-point widening of the SES math gap in 2022 relative to the pre-pandemic trend). This indicates that COVID-19 remote-learning conditions disproportionately harmed socioeconomically disadvantaged students in Taiwan, implying that post-pandemic recovery should prioritize targeted math catch-up and digital-access support for lower-SES learners, while recognizing that the paper does not report PV-combination and missing-data procedures in detail.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes OECD PISA Taiwan data for math achievement across six cycles (2006, 2009, 2012, 2015, 2018, 2022), focusing on students in the bottom vs top quarter of ESCS to define lower- and higher-SES groups. Using a difference-in-differences design with year fixed effects and controls (grade, gender, immigrant background, setting, public/private, and general/vocational), the paper finds that the SES math gap widened in 2022: in the fully specified DID model, the Lower×Post interaction is β = -26.110 (s.e. 7.928), p < 0.01, corresponding to roughly a one-year learning loss magnitude per OECD scaling. Descriptively, lower-SES students declined by about 10 points from pre- to post-pandemic, while higher-SES students increased by about 7.6 points. The analysis is not an ML predictive modeling study (no ML algorithms are trained), and the manuscript does not report how plausible values were combined or how missing data were handled, limiting full transparency of inference.
